stem: If $X=\{1, 2, 3, \dots, {=n}\}$ and R is a relation on X where $a\,R\,b$ means: «$b = a + {=k}$» for each of $a, b\in X$. When R is represented by an arrow diagram, how many arrows are drawn? (Each ordered pair of R is one arrow.)
solution: An arrow goes from a to b exactly when $(a, b)\in R$, that is when $b = a + {=k}$ and both a and b belong to X.
The first pair is $(1, {=k + 1})$ and the last pair is $({=n - k}, {=n})$, because a + {=k} must not exceed {=n}.
So a takes the values $1, 2, \dots, {=n - k}$, giving {=c} ordered pairs and therefore {=c} arrows.
notes: Basic entry: reading a relation on one set as ordered pairs / arrows. Numeric count to avoid set-of-pairs marker.
